content: The program ensures meaningful engagement at all stages of the intervention cycle. To effectively target interventions, hotspot areas were identified in collaboration with community leaders and service providers, who were trained to deliver non-judgmental and appropriate services for key populations. Focus group discussions and client exit interviews with members of key populations informed the design of the innovative program. Engagement with bar owners and staff facilitated their support, leading to the installation of convenient dispensers for condoms and lubricants. Clients diagnosed with HIV through LVCT Health testing services are promptly linked to treatment and care services. Data on HIV risk factors, STI types, and HIV status are entered into a national database, and cohort data is analyzed to identify trends, such as HIV prevalence by geographic location. Female sex workers undergo routine screening for STIs and cervical cancer using visual inspection methods, with immediate diagnosis provided. Those with lesions are referred to specialized centers for further management. Male sex workers are screened for STIs and other lesions, offered on-site syndromic management, and followed up in facility settings. LVCT Health reaches approximately 5,000 key population clients annually with HIV and sexual and reproductive health services, with over 80% of HIV-positive clients effectively linked to post-test services. The organization has achieved over 85% retention in care and treatment for men who have sex with men (MSM) and over 90% adherence to HAART. LVCT Health’s advocacy has led to the inclusion of key population issues in Kenya’s HIV National Strategic Plan, paving the way for potential national scale-up of services. Consistent follow-up with mobile populations is conducted through telephone calls by counselors and static sites near hotspots for follow-up services or unscheduled appointments. Collaboration with the Ministry of Health and security agencies addresses challenges in insecure locations, ensuring the safety of staff and clients. The National Organization of Peer Educators (NOPE) provides sexual and reproductive health and social services in diverse settings. NOPE developed the Drop-In Service Centre (DiSC) model as a one-stop approach for delivering essential HIV services to female sex workers (FSWs) and MSM in seven locations across Kisii and Kiambu counties. Consultations and focus group discussions with FSW and MSM community members identified service gaps, followed by social and hotspot mapping and population size estimations. Stakeholder meetings, including bar owners, police, provincial administrators, religious and community leaders, and FSW and MSM representatives, were held in identified hotspots to provide project information and encourage community buy-in. FSWs and MSM participated in selecting DiSC locations. Peer educators were trained to manage DiSCs, including setup, client flowcharts, referral pathways, and minimum service packages. NOPE collaborated with District Health Management Teams to source commodities and ensure service quality. NOPE follows a performance-monitoring plan aligned with the national AIDS strategic plan and PEPFAR indicators. Routine data quality assessments, audits, supervision visits, data-sharing forums, and project progress meetings ensure robust monitoring and evaluation mechanisms. DiSCs have served 20,000 individuals from FSW and MSM communities. Based on this experience, NOPE has contributed to national guidelines for key populations and developed the national MSM peer education curriculum. Technical assistance from NOPE has enabled organizations like Ishtar MSM and Keeping Alive Societies’ Hope to take over three DiSCs. A key lesson from establishing DiSCs is the importance of gaining the trust of key populations, especially in environments where laws and policies criminalize FSWs and MSM. While standalone facilities are critical for key populations, sustainability will require integrating service delivery into national health services as communities and providers become more responsive to their needs. In the meantime, NOPE has mobilized county health management teams to provide medical supplies and second medical staff to DiSCs. The Marsa Sexual Health Centre in Beirut offers sexual and reproductive health services in a welcoming, stigma-free environment, targeting young people, unmarried sexually active women, and marginalized communities, including MSM and transgender individuals. Ensuring client anonymity and confidentiality is key to encouraging service uptake. Clients are assigned unique file numbers, and they decide whether to provide additional identifying information. Experienced and sensitized staff maintain confidentiality, fostering trust and openness among clients. Marsa does not advertise publicly but uses social media, the internet, street outreach campaigns, and word-of-mouth to share information about its services. Médecins du Monde (MdM) implements a project in Yangon and Kachin State, Myanmar, focusing on STI and HIV prevention, treatment, care, and harm reduction for FSWs, MSM, and people who use drugs. The program provides comprehensive, high-quality services free of charge at drop-in centers and clinics run by MdM. It was developed in close collaboration with key populations, with peers playing a crucial role in ensuring the program meets their needs. MdM has observed a steady decrease in HIV prevalence among MSM, people who use drugs, and sex workers in Myanmar. However, in rural areas with limited access to primary healthcare, offering a wide range of health services to people who use drugs can be challenging. Addressing basic health needs alongside those of key populations can strengthen program acceptance and reduce misunderstandings. The greatest challenge is fostering local NGOs and community-based groups to take over harm reduction efforts currently dependent on international NGOs. Beyond service delivery, skills transfer and capacity building are becoming priorities in Myanmar. The Naz Male Health Alliance (NMHA) in Pakistan addresses the health and psychosocial needs of young MSM and transgender individuals. Operating six service delivery centers in five cities, NMHA serves 47,000 registered clients. Each site includes a clinic and a drop-in center, providing a safe and relaxing environment for low-income MSM and transgender clients. Centers are strategically located near MSM hotspots and hijra deras (transgender dwellings). Drop-in centers and outreach activities complement each other, establishing long-term client relationships and linking them to services. Each center has a multidisciplinary staff of around 15, including STI specialists, psychologists, and peer educators, with over 95% of staff being MSM or transgender individuals. The Government of Pakistan credits NMHA with significantly increasing the number of newly registered HIV-positive MSM and transgender individuals in public HIV treatment centers. NMHA builds strong partnerships with organizations like the National AIDS Control Programme and international coalitions to enhance its impact. In South Africa, a multi-partner project led by SANAC and the Department of Health has developed an integrated approach to sensitize healthcare providers on key population issues and empower public health staff to interact appropriately with these communities. Training sessions have improved healthcare workers’ attitudes, increased community trust, and boosted the use of health facilities. Further evaluation is planned to inform scale-up. Kimara Peers, a community-based NGO in Dar es Salaam, operates two drop-in centers near state-run health facilities to serve people who use drugs, including young sex workers. Services include psychosocial therapy, harm reduction education, STI prevention, and referrals for methadone therapy. Confidentiality is maintained, and referrals to government hospitals are made only with the client’s consent. The program seeks government approval to provide clean needles and syringes. Save the Children uses ICT to enhance HIV prevention outreach to MSM and transgender individuals in Chiang Mai, Thailand. The project leverages social media platforms like Facebook and Line to provide information on HIV prevention, treatment, and care. Outreach workers use tablets to engage clients, show project content, and record contact details for follow-up. Continued online contact helps build trust with counselors, encouraging service uptake.
